claims.statement: Inflation describes an increase in the general price level across the economy.
primary_sources: International Monetary Fund (IMF) - What is Inflation?
Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Consumer Price Index Methodology
claims.qualification: Inflation measures the aggregate change in prices of a basket of consumer goods and services, rather than a uniform increase across every single individual product.

claims.statement: Purchasing power describes the quantity of goods and services that can be purchased with a given unit or nominal amount of money.
primary_sources: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED Economic Data)
claims.qualification: When the general price level rises, each monetary unit buys fewer goods and services; hence, purchasing power declines.

claims.statement: At a constant 3% annual compound inflation rate, the general price level rises by approximately 80.6% over 20 years (factor (1.03)^20 ≈ 1.8061).
claims.qualification: Hypothetical illustration assuming annual compounding without mid-year fluctuations. Not an economic forecast.

claims.statement: A basket of goods priced at $100.00 today would cost $180.61 after 20 years under a constant 3% annual inflation rate.
claims.qualification: Assumes identical basket composition across 20 years. Subject to substitution effects in real consumer behavior.

claims.statement: The purchasing power of a fixed $100.00 banknote after 20 years, measured in today's base-year dollars, shrinks to $55.37.
claims.qualification: Nominal money remains $100.00; real purchasing power contracts by 44.63%.

claims.statement: Money is not just about the nominal amount possessed; it is fundamentally about what that money can buy.
primary_sources: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776) - Nominal vs Real Price
Irving Fisher, The Purchasing Power of Money (1911)
claims.qualification: Core philosophical takeaway emphasizing real versus nominal economic values.

disclaimers.text: Hypothetical 3% annual compound inflation model over 20 years. Illustrative of price-level effects; individual goods and actual inflation rates vary. Educational analysis only, not financial advice.
